name: Auditing Smart Contracts
title: Auditing Smart Contracts
answer: Auditing smart contracts is the review of self-executing code on a blockchain to find defects, security flaws, and mismatches between what the code does and what its users or owners believe it does. It covers token contracts, decentralized finance protocols, bridges, governance systems, and any on-chain logic that holds or moves value. In digital asset accounting, the audit also asks whether the contract's events and balances can be relied on for financial reporting, tax, and reconciliation. The work sits between software assurance, security testing, and financial statement audit, and it often requires reading both code and the economic design behind it.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Auditing smart contracts is the review of self-executing code on a blockchain to find defects, security flaws, and mismatches between what the code does and what its users or owners believe it does. It covers token contracts, decentralized finance protocols, bridges, governance systems, and any on-chain logic that holds or moves value. In digital asset accounting, the audit also asks whether the contract's events and balances can be relied on for financial reporting, tax, and reconciliation. The work sits between software assurance, security testing, and financial statement audit, and it often requires reading both code and the economic design behind it.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Smart contract audits run on the same public or permissioned blockchains that host the contracts, most often Ethereum and compatible EVM networks, with other chains such as Solana or Cosmos requiring different tooling. Auditors use local development environments like Foundry or Hardhat to compile, test, and simulate contracts, and they read bytecode and source code from block explorers and repositories. Static analysis tools such as Slither and Mythril, fuzzers such as Echidna, and formal verification tools help surface common flaws, but they do not replace manual review. The infrastructure also includes forked mainnet states, so an auditor can replay real conditions without spending real assets.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually starts with scoping the contracts, the deployment scripts, and the privileges held by admin keys or governance. Auditors then combine manual line by line review with automated static analysis, unit tests, fuzzing, and symbolic execution, and they check access control, arithmetic, reentrancy, oracle use, and upgrade patterns. They trace value flows across contracts and compare the code's behavior to the stated intent, including edge cases like paused markets or failed liquidations. Findings are written up with severity, proof of concept, and recommended fixes, and a re audit confirms whether the fixes hold. For accounting purposes, the auditor may also test whether emitted events are complete and consistent enough to support ledger entries.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in smart contract auditing turn on who can change the contract, who can pause it, and who bears loss when a flaw is exploited. Provenance matters because an audit report is tied to a specific commit, deployment address, and set of assumptions, and a later upgrade can invalidate it. Auditors often need confidentiality agreements, and some engagements require disclosure rules for critical findings before public deployment. Regulatory expectations are still forming, and attention to this area is growing. Insurance, bug bounties, and multisignature controls are common risk transfer and risk reduction measures, but none of them remove the underlying code risk.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward continuous auditing rather than one time reviews, with monitoring tools that watch live contracts for anomalous transactions. Formal verification and property based testing are becoming more practical for critical protocols, and AI assisted review is starting to help triage large codebases, though human judgment remains central. Accountants and auditors will likely need to connect on chain evidence to traditional audit trails, including attestations, proofs, and standardized event schemas. As tokenization spreads, smart contract audit reports may become a routine input to digital asset accounting and disclosure. The open question is how to keep audit assurance current when the code and its governance can change after the report is signed.
